sections.text:
Paul compares himself to a mother. When he first came to Thessalonica, he says, “we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.” It is a tender picture from a man who had to leave this young church in a hurry, and who writes to them now with feeling.

He gives thanks for their faith under pressure and recalls his time with them. When Timothy brings a good report, Paul is relieved. He encourages them to live holy lives and to keep working quietly.

Then he turns to a grief the church is carrying: some believers have died. Paul writes so that they will not grieve like people with no hope. When the Lord returns, “The dead in Christ will rise first,” and all will be with him forever. No one knows when that day will come, so they are told, “let’s watch and be sober.”

Thessalonica was the chief city of Macedonia. Paul founded the church there on his second journey (Acts 17) and wrote from Corinth around the year 50 or 51. It is among the earliest of his letters, and of the whole New Testament.

The passage about being caught up to meet the Lord (4:17) is the main basis for the teaching called the rapture. Some Christians expect believers to be taken before a period of great trouble. Many others read it as part of the single return of Christ, with believers going out to welcome him. Both sides take the passage seriously, and both start from the same comfort the letter offers: that those who have died are not lost.
